subject.name: Chemistry
subject.overview: ICSE Class 9 Chemistry builds the working vocabulary of the subject: symbols, valency, chemical formulae and balanced equations, followed by the main types of chemical reactions and the energy changes that go with them. Students study water as a solvent and the ideas of hydrated, deliquescent and efflorescent substances, then move to atomic structure, electronic configuration and ionic and covalent bonding. The periodic table, the chemistry of hydrogen, the gas laws and atmospheric pollution complete the course. Almost every Class 10 chapter, including mole concept, electrolysis, acids, bases and salts and the study of compounds, assumes fluency with formulae, equations, valency and periodic trends learnt here, so gaps in Class 9 show up quickly in Class 10.
studyTips: Memorise the symbols and valencies of common elements and radicals (such as NH₄⁺, NO₃⁻, SO₄²⁻, CO₃²⁻, PO₄³⁻) until you can write any formula by the criss-cross method without hesitation.
Practise balancing equations daily and always check that atoms of every element are equal on both sides; add state symbols and conditions where they are relevant.
For periodic trends, learn the reason (nuclear charge, number of shells, shielding) along with the trend, because answers are marked on the explanation, not just the direction.
In gas-law numericals, convert every temperature to kelvin first, keep pressure and volume units consistent, and write the formula before substituting values.
Keep a single sheet of laboratory observations (colour changes, gases evolved, precipitates formed) and revise it regularly, since observation-based questions are common.

chapters.name: The Language of Chemistry
chapters.summary: Covers symbols of elements, valency of elements and radicals, writing chemical formulae, calculating molecular mass and percentage composition, and writing and balancing chemical equations.

chapters.name: Chemical Changes and Reactions
chapters.summary: Describes the conditions needed for chemical reactions, the characteristics by which they are recognised, the main types of reactions, and the energy changes (exothermic and endothermic) that accompany them.

topics.name: Conditions and characteristics of chemical reactions

chapters.name: Water
chapters.summary: Deals with water as a universal solvent, solubility of solids and gases, water of crystallisation, hydrated, anhydrous, deliquescent, efflorescent and hygroscopic substances, and hard and soft water.

topics.name: Water as a solvent and solubility

chapters.name: Atomic Structure and Chemical Bonding
chapters.summary: Explains the fundamental particles of the atom, the atomic models of Thomson, Rutherford and Bohr, electronic configuration, isotopes and isobars, and how atoms combine through ionic (electrovalent) and covalent bonds.

chapters.name: The Periodic Table
chapters.summary: Traces the classification of elements from Dobereiner, Newlands and Mendeleev to the Modern Periodic Law, and studies groups, periods and periodic trends, with special reference to alkali metals and halogens.

topics.name: Modern periodic law and the long form table

chapters.name: Study of the First Element — Hydrogen
chapters.summary: Covers the position of hydrogen in the periodic table, its preparation from water, acids and alkalis, its laboratory and industrial (Bosch process) preparation, its properties and uses, and oxidation and reduction.

topics.name: Position of hydrogen in the periodic table

chapters.name: Study of Gas Laws
chapters.summary: Introduces the kinetic theory of gases, Boyle's law, Charles's law, the absolute (Kelvin) scale of temperature, the combined gas equation and standard temperature and pressure (STP).

topics.name: Kinetic theory and behaviour of gases

chapters.name: Atmospheric Pollution
chapters.summary: Discusses acid rain, the greenhouse effect and global warming, and depletion of the ozone layer, including their causes, effects and preventive measures.

questions.text: What is the valency of the sulphate radical (SO₄)?
questions.answer: 2 — the sulphate ion is SO₄²⁻.
questions.explanation: The sulphate radical carries a charge of −2, so its valency is 2, as in Na₂SO₄ and CaSO₄.

questions.text: The chemical formula of calcium nitrate is ____.
questions.answer: Ca(NO₃)₂
questions.explanation: Calcium has valency 2 and the nitrate radical has valency 1, so two nitrate groups are needed.

questions.text: Calculate the molecular mass of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃. (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
questions.answer: Molecular mass of CaCO₃ = 40 + 12 + (3 × 16) = 40 + 12 + 48 = 100 u.
questions.explanation: Add the atomic masses of all atoms present, multiplying by the number of each kind of atom.

questions.text: Calculate the percentage of nitrogen in ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃. (N = 14, H = 1, O = 16)
questions.answer: Molecular mass of NH₄NO₃ = 14 + 4(1) + 14 + 3(16) = 80. Mass of nitrogen = 2 × 14 = 28. Percentage of N = (28 ÷ 80) × 100 = 35%.
questions.explanation: Ammonium nitrate contains two nitrogen atoms, one in NH₄⁺ and one in NO₃⁻.

questions.text:
Balance the following equations:
(a) Fe + H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + H₂
(b) Al + O₂ → Al₂O₃
(c) NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O
questions.answer:
(a) 3Fe + 4H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂
(b) 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃
(c) 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O
(1 mark each)
questions.explanation: In each case the number of atoms of every element is equal on both sides after balancing.

questions.text:
(a) Define valency. What is meant by variable valency? Illustrate with one example. (2)
(b) Write the chemical formulae of: (i) aluminium sulphate (ii) ammonium phosphate (iii) iron(III) hydroxide (iv) potassium dichromate. (2)
questions.answer:
(a) Valency is the combining capacity of an atom or radical, i.e. the number of hydrogen atoms (or twice the number of oxygen atoms) with which one atom of the element combines, or the number of electrons it loses, gains or shares during bond formation. Some elements show more than one valency; this is called variable valency. Example: iron shows valency 2 in iron(II)/ferrous compounds such as FeSO₄ and valency 3 in iron(III)/ferric compounds such as FeCl₃. (Copper, Cu⁺/Cu²⁺, is also acceptable.)
(b) (i) Al₂(SO₄)₃ (ii) (NH₄)₃PO₄ (iii) Fe(OH)₃ (iv) K₂Cr₂O₇ (½ mark each)
questions.explanation: Formulae are obtained by exchanging the valencies of the positive and negative parts (criss-cross method) and simplifying where possible.

questions.text: The reaction CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, which occurs on strong heating, is an example of:
questions.answer: Thermal decomposition
questions.explanation: A single compound breaks down into simpler substances when heated.

questions.text: A chemical reaction in which heat is absorbed from the surroundings is called an ____ reaction.
questions.answer: endothermic
questions.explanation: Example: N₂ + O₂ → 2NO absorbs heat.

questions.text: Distinguish between a displacement reaction and a double decomposition reaction, giving one balanced equation for each.
questions.answer:
Displacement: a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound, e.g. Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu.
Double decomposition: two compounds exchange their radicals/ions to form two new compounds, e.g. AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl↓ + NaNO₃.
(1 mark each)
questions.explanation: In displacement one element replaces another; in double decomposition two compounds swap partners.

questions.text: Other than heat, state two conditions that can bring about a chemical reaction. Give one example of each.
questions.answer:
Any two, with example:
• Light: silver bromide decomposes in light, 2AgBr → 2Ag + Br₂ (or photosynthesis).
• Catalyst: potassium chlorate decomposes faster with MnO₂, 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂.
• Electricity: water decomposes on passing current, 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂.
• Close contact / solution: solid AgNO₃ and NaCl react readily only when dissolved in water.
• Pressure: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ is favoured by high pressure.
questions.explanation: Reactions need the reactants to come into contact and often need an energy input or a catalyst.

questions.text: Give one balanced equation for a reaction in which: (a) a white precipitate is formed, (b) a change of colour is observed, (c) a gas is evolved.
questions.answer:
(a) BaCl₂ + Na₂SO₄ → BaSO₄↓ (white) + 2NaCl
(b) Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu; the blue solution turns pale green and a reddish-brown deposit of copper forms.
(c) Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂↑
(Other correct examples are acceptable; 1 mark each.)
questions.explanation: Precipitation, colour change and gas evolution are common observable characteristics of chemical reactions.

questions.text:
(a) Explain the terms exothermic and endothermic reactions, with one balanced equation for each. (2)
(b) Classify each reaction by type: (i) 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂ (in presence of MnO₂, on heating) (ii) NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O (iii) N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (iv) 2AgBr → 2Ag + Br₂ (in sunlight). (2)
questions.answer:
(a) Exothermic reaction: heat is released to the surroundings, e.g. C + O₂ → CO₂ + heat. Endothermic reaction: heat is absorbed from the surroundings, e.g. N₂ + O₂ → 2NO − heat (or CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ on heating). (1 mark each)
(b) (i) Thermal decomposition (catalysed) (ii) Neutralisation (a double decomposition) (iii) Combination (reversible, direct synthesis) (iv) Photochemical decomposition (½ mark each)
questions.explanation: The energy term shows whether heat is a product (exothermic) or needs to be supplied (endothermic).

questions.text: Which of the following substances is deliquescent?
questions.answer: Anhydrous calcium chloride
questions.explanation: It absorbs so much moisture from the air that it dissolves in it and forms a solution.

questions.text: In blue vitriol, CuSO₄·xH₂O, the value of x (number of molecules of water of crystallisation) is ____.
questions.answer: 5 (CuSO₄·5H₂O)
questions.explanation: Blue vitriol is copper(II) sulphate pentahydrate.

questions.text: Crystals of washing soda left open in dry air lose mass and turn into a white powder. Name this property and write the equation for the change.
questions.answer: The property is efflorescence. Washing soda crystals lose part of their water of crystallisation to the atmosphere: Na₂CO₃·10H₂O → Na₂CO₃·H₂O + 9H₂O.
questions.explanation: Efflorescent substances give out water of crystallisation when exposed to dry air.

questions.text: Distinguish between temporary and permanent hardness of water, stating the cause of each and one method of removing each, with an equation.
questions.answer:
Temporary hardness is caused by dissolved bicarbonates of calcium and magnesium. It is removed by boiling: Ca(HCO₃)₂ → CaCO₃↓ + H₂O + CO₂.
Permanent hardness is caused by dissolved chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium. It is removed by adding washing soda: CaCl₂ + Na₂CO₃ → CaCO₃↓ + 2NaCl (or MgSO₄ + Na₂CO₃ → MgCO₃↓ + Na₂SO₄).
questions.explanation: Boiling decomposes bicarbonates, but chlorides and sulphates are not affected by boiling.

questions.text:
(a) Why is water called a universal solvent? (1)
(b) How does the solubility of a gas in water change with a rise in temperature? Why is this important for aquatic life? (1)
(c) Define water of crystallisation. Describe what is observed when blue copper sulphate crystals are heated, and when water is then added to the residue. (2)
(d) Why is anhydrous calcium chloride used as a drying agent? (1)
questions.answer:
(a) Water dissolves a larger number of substances than any other solvent, because its molecules are polar and can surround and separate ions and many polar molecules.
(b) The solubility of a gas decreases as temperature rises. Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, so aquatic organisms may not get enough oxygen.
(c) Water of crystallisation is the fixed number of water molecules chemically combined with one formula unit of a salt in its crystalline form. On heating, blue CuSO₄·5H₂O loses its water and becomes white anhydrous CuSO₄ (water droplets appear on the cooler parts of the tube). On adding water, the white powder turns blue again with the evolution of heat.
(d) It is hygroscopic (in fact deliquescent): it readily absorbs moisture, so it removes water vapour from gases and substances kept with it.
questions.explanation: The reversible colour change of copper sulphate is also used as a test for water.

questions.text: Which fundamental particle of an atom carries no electric charge?
questions.answer: Neutron
questions.explanation: Protons are positive and electrons are negative; neutrons are electrically neutral.

questions.text: Isotopes of an element differ from each other in the number of:
questions.answer: Neutrons
questions.explanation: Isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass numbers because they contain different numbers of neutrons.

questions.text: The maximum number of electrons that can be accommodated in the M shell is ____.
questions.explanation: Maximum electrons in a shell = 2n²; for the M shell n = 3, so 2 × 9 = 18.

questions.text: The electronic configuration of the magnesium ion, Mg²⁺ (atomic number of Mg = 12), is:
questions.explanation: Magnesium (2, 8, 2) loses its two valence electrons to form Mg²⁺ with 10 electrons.

questions.text: An atom of chlorine, ³⁵₁₇Cl, contains ____ neutrons.
questions.explanation: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 35 − 17 = 18.

questions.text: State two conclusions Rutherford drew from his alpha-particle scattering experiment.
questions.answer:
Any two:
• Most of the space inside an atom is empty, since most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil.
• The positive charge and almost all the mass of the atom are concentrated in a very small central region called the nucleus, since a few particles were deflected through large angles.
• The nucleus is extremely small compared with the size of the atom, since very few particles bounced back.
questions.explanation: These observations led to the nuclear model of the atom.

questions.text: Naturally occurring chlorine contains 75% of the isotope ³⁵Cl and 25% of the isotope ³⁷Cl. Calculate the average atomic mass of chlorine.
questions.explanation: The average atomic mass is the weighted mean of the isotopic masses, which is why chlorine's atomic mass is fractional.

questions.text: What are isobars? Give one pair of isobars, stating their atomic numbers and mass number.
questions.answer: Isobars are atoms of different elements that have the same mass number but different atomic numbers. Example: argon, ⁴⁰₁₈Ar, and calcium, ⁴⁰₂₀Ca — both have mass number 40, with atomic numbers 18 and 20.
questions.explanation: Isobars have the same total number of nucleons but different numbers of protons, so they are different elements.

questions.text: State three postulates of Bohr's model of the atom.
questions.answer:
Any three:
• Electrons revolve around the nucleus in fixed circular paths called orbits, shells or energy levels (K, L, M, N… or n = 1, 2, 3, 4…).
• Each orbit has a definite energy; energy increases as the distance from the nucleus increases.
• While an electron remains in a given orbit it does not lose or gain energy (these are stationary states).
• An electron absorbs energy when it jumps to a higher orbit and emits energy when it returns to a lower orbit; the energy absorbed or emitted equals the difference in energy between the two levels.
questions.explanation: Bohr's model explained why electrons do not spiral into the nucleus, a problem with Rutherford's model.

questions.text: Explain the formation of magnesium chloride, MgCl₂, in terms of electron transfer. (Atomic numbers: Mg = 12, Cl = 17)
questions.answer: Mg has configuration 2, 8, 2 and Cl has 2, 8, 7. A magnesium atom loses its two valence electrons to form Mg²⁺ (2, 8), attaining the stable neon configuration: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻. Each of two chlorine atoms gains one electron to form Cl⁻ (2, 8, 8), attaining the argon configuration: 2Cl + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻. The oppositely charged ions are held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction, forming the ionic (electrovalent) compound Mg²⁺(Cl⁻)₂, i.e. MgCl₂.
questions.explanation: One magnesium atom transfers one electron to each of two chlorine atoms.

questions.text: Give three differences between the properties of ionic (electrovalent) compounds and covalent compounds.
questions.answer:
Any three:
• State: ionic compounds are usually crystalline solids; covalent compounds may be gases, liquids or soft solids.
• Melting and boiling points: high for ionic compounds (strong electrostatic forces); generally low for covalent compounds (weak intermolecular forces).
• Electrical conductivity: ionic compounds conduct electricity in the molten state or aqueous solution; covalent compounds generally do not conduct.
• Solubility: ionic compounds usually dissolve in water and are insoluble in organic solvents; covalent compounds are usually insoluble in water but dissolve in organic solvents.
• Ionic compounds are made of ions; covalent compounds are made of molecules.
questions.explanation: The differences arise from the nature of the particles and the forces between them.

questions.text:
An element X has atomic number 8 and mass number 16.
(a) Write its electronic configuration. (1)
(b) State its valency. (1)
(c) How many protons and neutrons are present in its nucleus? (1)
(d) What type of bond will X form with hydrogen? Name the compound formed. (1)
questions.answer:
(a) 2, 6
(b) Valency = 2 (it needs 2 electrons to complete its octet).
(c) Protons = 8; neutrons = 16 − 8 = 8.
(d) A covalent bond (two single covalent bonds formed by sharing of electron pairs). The compound is water, H₂O (X is oxygen).
questions.explanation: Valency of a non-metal = 8 − number of valence electrons = 8 − 6 = 2.

questions.text:
(a) Describe, with electron-dot reasoning, the bonding in (i) a nitrogen molecule, N₂, and (ii) a methane molecule, CH₄. (Atomic numbers: N = 7, C = 6, H = 1) (2)
(b) State the octet rule. (1)
(c) Why are noble gases chemically unreactive? (1)
questions.answer:
(a) (i) Each N atom (2, 5) has 5 valence electrons and needs 3 more. The two N atoms share three pairs of electrons, forming a triple covalent bond, N≡N; each N then has 8 electrons in its outer shell and one lone pair.
(ii) Carbon (2, 4) has 4 valence electrons and needs 4 more; each H atom has 1 electron and needs 1 more. Carbon shares one electron pair with each of four H atoms, forming four single covalent bonds. Carbon attains an octet and each hydrogen attains a duplet.
(b) Atoms combine by losing, gaining or sharing electrons so as to acquire 8 electrons in their outermost shell (2 in the case of the first shell, the duplet), i.e. the stable configuration of the nearest noble gas.
(c) Noble gases already have a stable, completely filled outermost shell (octet; duplet in helium), so they have no tendency to lose, gain or share electrons.
questions.explanation: Covalent bonds are formed by sharing electron pairs between non-metal atoms.

questions.text:
Element A has atomic number 20 and element B has atomic number 8.
(a) Write the electronic configurations of A and B. (1)
(b) Which of the two is a metal? Give a reason. (1)
(c) Write the formula of the compound formed between A and B and name the type of bond. (1)
(d) Explain how the bond is formed in terms of electrons. (1)
(e) State two properties you would expect this compound to have. (1)
questions.answer:
(a) A: 2, 8, 8, 2; B: 2, 6
(b) A is a metal because it has 2 valence electrons which it tends to lose to form a positive ion.
(c) AB (A²⁺B²⁻); the bond is ionic (electrovalent). (A is calcium and B is oxygen, so the compound is CaO.)
(d) Atom A loses its two valence electrons to form A²⁺ (2, 8, 8); atom B gains these two electrons to form B²⁻ (2, 8). The oppositely charged ions are held together by strong electrostatic attraction.
(e) Any two: it is a hard crystalline solid; it has a high melting and boiling point; it conducts electricity in the molten state; it is not a conductor in the solid state.
questions.explanation: Metals with 1–3 valence electrons form ionic bonds with non-metals that need 1–3 electrons.

questions.text: The Modern Periodic Law states that the properties of elements are a periodic function of their:
questions.answer: Atomic numbers
questions.explanation: Moseley showed that atomic number, not atomic mass, is the fundamental property of an element.

questions.text: On moving from left to right across a period (excluding noble gases), the atomic size of elements generally:
questions.answer: Decreases
questions.explanation: Nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell, so the electrons are pulled closer to the nucleus.

questions.text: The horizontal rows of the modern periodic table are called ____.
questions.answer: periods
questions.explanation: There are 7 periods; the vertical columns are called groups.

questions.text: Which of the following halogens is the most reactive?
questions.answer: Fluorine
questions.explanation: Fluorine has the smallest atoms, so it attracts an extra electron most strongly; reactivity of halogens decreases down the group.

questions.text: In Dobereiner's triad of lithium (atomic mass 7), sodium and potassium (atomic mass 39), the atomic mass of sodium is approximately ____.
questions.explanation: In a triad, the middle element's atomic mass is roughly the mean of the other two: (7 + 39) ÷ 2 = 23.

questions.text: State Newlands' law of octaves and give one of its limitations.
questions.answer:
Law of octaves: when elements are arranged in increasing order of atomic mass, every eighth element has properties similar to the first, like the eighth note of a musical scale.
Limitation (any one): it held good only up to calcium; it could not accommodate elements discovered later or the noble gases; in some places dissimilar elements were placed together (e.g. iron with oxygen and sulphur).
questions.explanation: The pattern broke down for heavier elements.

questions.text: An element has the electronic configuration 2, 8, 3. State its period number and group number, giving a reason for each.
questions.answer:
Period 3, because its electrons occupy three shells.
Group 13 (IIIA), because it has 3 valence electrons. (The element is aluminium.)
questions.explanation: Period number = number of shells; for groups 1, 2 and 13–17, the valence electrons fix the group.

questions.text: State two merits of Mendeleev's periodic table.
questions.answer:
Any two:
• He left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties (e.g. eka-aluminium and eka-silicon, later discovered as gallium and germanium).
• He corrected the doubtful atomic masses of some elements (e.g. beryllium).
• It grouped elements with similar properties together, which made the study of elements systematic.
• Noble gases, discovered later, could be placed in a separate group without disturbing the arrangement.
questions.explanation: The accurate prediction of new elements was the strongest evidence for Mendeleev's table.

questions.text: Define ionisation potential (ionisation energy). How does it change (a) across a period from left to right and (b) down a group? Give a reason for each.
questions.answer:
Ionisation potential is the energy required to remove the most loosely held electron from an isolated gaseous atom of an element.
(a) It generally increases across a period, because nuclear charge increases and atomic size decreases, so valence electrons are held more tightly.
(b) It decreases down a group, because atomic size increases with the addition of new shells and the valence electrons are farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so they are removed more easily.
questions.explanation: Ionisation potential is inversely related to atomic size.

questions.text: Give three characteristic properties shared by the alkali metals (Group 1). Include one balanced equation.
questions.answer:
Any three:
• They have one valence electron and a valency of 1.
• They readily lose that electron to form unipositive ions (Na⁺, K⁺) and are strong reducing agents.
• They react vigorously with cold water to form an alkali and hydrogen: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂↑.
• They are soft metals with low densities and low melting points.
• Their reactivity increases down the group.
questions.explanation: Similar properties arise from the same number of valence electrons.

questions.text: How does metallic character change (a) across a period from left to right and (b) down a group? Explain each trend in terms of atomic structure.
questions.answer:
Metallic character is the tendency of an atom to lose electrons and form positive ions.
(a) It decreases across a period: nuclear charge increases and atomic size decreases, so the atom loses electrons less readily (elements change from metals to metalloids to non-metals).
(b) It increases down a group: atomic size increases with the addition of shells, so valence electrons are farther from the nucleus and are lost more easily.
questions.explanation: Metallic character follows the ease with which valence electrons are lost.

questions.text:
Consider the Period 2 elements: Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F.
(a) Which has the largest atomic radius? (1)
(b) Which is the most electronegative? (1)
(c) Which one is a metalloid? (1)
(d) What is the valency of nitrogen in its compound with hydrogen, and what is the formula of that compound? (1)
questions.answer:
(a) Lithium (Li)
(b) Fluorine (F)
(c) Boron (B)
(d) Valency 3; the compound is ammonia, NH₃.
questions.explanation: Atomic radius decreases and electronegativity increases across a period; nitrogen (2, 5) needs 3 electrons to complete its octet.

questions.text:
(a) Write the electronic configuration of chlorine (atomic number 17) and explain why it is placed in Group 17. (1)
(b) How does the reactivity of halogens change down the group? Give a reason. (1)
(c) Chlorine gas is bubbled through potassium bromide solution. Write the balanced equation and explain why iodine cannot displace chlorine from potassium chloride. (1)
(d) How does the physical state of halogens change from fluorine to iodine at room temperature? (1)
questions.answer:
(a) 2, 8, 7. It has 7 valence electrons, so it belongs to Group 17 (VIIA).
(b) Reactivity decreases down the group, because atomic size increases and the tendency of the atom to gain an electron decreases.
(c) Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂. Chlorine is more reactive than bromine and iodine, so a less reactive halogen (iodine) cannot displace a more reactive one (chlorine) from its salt.
(d) Fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid and iodine is a solid.
questions.explanation: A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from its salt solution.

questions.text: Which of these metals reacts with cold water to liberate hydrogen gas?
questions.answer: Sodium
questions.explanation: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂; iron reacts only with steam, and copper does not react with water.

questions.text: In the laboratory, hydrogen is prepared by the action of granulated zinc on dilute ____ acid.
questions.answer: hydrochloric (dilute sulphuric acid is also acceptable)
questions.explanation: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂↑. Nitric acid is not used because it is an oxidising agent.

questions.text: In the laboratory preparation of hydrogen, why is the gas collected by the downward displacement of water and not by displacement of air?
questions.answer: Hydrogen is only sparingly soluble in water, so it can be collected over water without loss. It is not collected by displacement of air because hydrogen forms an explosive mixture with air, and it is difficult to judge when all the air has been expelled.
questions.explanation: Collecting over water also gives a purer sample.

questions.text: For the reaction CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, identify: (a) the substance oxidised, (b) the substance reduced, (c) the oxidising agent, (d) the reducing agent.
questions.answer:
(a) Hydrogen (H₂) is oxidised to water.
(b) Copper(II) oxide (CuO) is reduced to copper.
(c) Oxidising agent: CuO
(d) Reducing agent: H₂
(½ mark each)
questions.explanation: Hydrogen gains oxygen (oxidation) while copper oxide loses oxygen (reduction).

questions.text: Hydrogen resembles both alkali metals and halogens. Give two resemblances with alkali metals and one resemblance with halogens.
questions.answer:
With alkali metals (any two):
• It has one electron in its outermost shell (H: 1; Na: 2, 8, 1).
• It can lose this electron to form a positive ion, H⁺, and has valency 1.
• It acts as a reducing agent, like alkali metals.
• It combines with non-metals such as oxygen and chlorine to form compounds with similar formulae (H₂O/Na₂O, HCl/NaCl).
With halogens (any one):
• It needs one electron to attain the stable configuration of the nearest noble gas (helium) and can form a negative ion, H⁻ (as in NaH).
• It exists as a diatomic molecule, H₂, like Cl₂.
• It is a non-metal and forms covalent compounds such as CH₄ (compare CCl₄).
questions.explanation: This dual nature is why the position of hydrogen in the periodic table is regarded as anomalous.

questions.text:
(a) Describe the manufacture of hydrogen by the Bosch process, giving balanced equations and the conditions used. (3)
(b) State two uses of hydrogen. (1)
questions.answer:
(a) Step 1: Steam is passed over white-hot coke (about 1000 °C) to form water gas: C + H₂O → CO + H₂ (endothermic).
Step 2: Water gas is mixed with excess steam and passed over a catalyst of iron(III) oxide (Fe₂O₃) with chromium(III) oxide as promoter at about 450 °C; carbon monoxide is converted to carbon dioxide: CO + H₂ + H₂O → CO₂ + 2H₂.
Step 3: The gas mixture is passed through water under pressure, which dissolves CO₂; remaining traces of CO are removed by passing through ammoniacal copper(I) chloride solution, leaving hydrogen.
(b) Any two: manufacture of ammonia (Haber process); hydrogenation of vegetable oils to make vanaspati ghee; as a fuel (e.g. liquid hydrogen in rockets); in the oxy-hydrogen flame for welding; as a reducing agent in extracting metals.
questions.explanation: The Bosch process uses cheap raw materials (coke and steam) to produce hydrogen on a large scale.

questions.text: Absolute zero (0 K) on the Celsius scale is approximately:
questions.explanation: T (K) = t (°C) + 273, so 0 K corresponds to −273 °C.

questions.text: A gas occupies 500 cm³ at a pressure of 760 mm of Hg. Calculate its volume when the pressure is reduced to 380 mm of Hg at constant temperature.
questions.answer: By Boyle's law, P₁V₁ = P₂V₂. V₂ = P₁V₁ ÷ P₂ = (760 × 500) ÷ 380 = 1000 cm³.
questions.explanation: Halving the pressure at constant temperature doubles the volume.

questions.text: A gas has a volume of 300 cm³ at 27 °C. Find its volume at 127 °C if the pressure remains constant.
questions.answer: T₁ = 27 + 273 = 300 K; T₂ = 127 + 273 = 400 K. By Charles's law, V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂, so V₂ = 300 × 400 ÷ 300 = 400 cm³.
questions.explanation: Temperatures must be converted to kelvin before applying Charles's law.

questions.text: A sample of gas occupies 380 cm³ at 27 °C and 800 mm of Hg. Calculate its volume at STP (0 °C and 760 mm of Hg).
questions.explanation: STP means 273 K and 760 mm of Hg (1 atm).

questions.text: A gas occupies 250 cm³ at 2 atm and 27 °C. To what temperature, in degrees Celsius, must it be brought so that it occupies 400 cm³ at 1.5 atm?
questions.explanation: Solve in kelvin and convert back to Celsius only at the end.

questions.text:
(a) State Boyle's law and Charles's law. (2)
(b) Using the kinetic theory of gases, explain why the pressure of a gas increases when its volume is decreased at constant temperature. (1)
(c) Why is the Kelvin scale used in gas-law calculations instead of the Celsius scale? (1)
(d) The Kelvin temperature of a fixed mass of gas is doubled at constant pressure. What happens to its volume? (1)
questions.answer:
(a) Boyle's law: at constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of a gas is inversely proportional to its pressure (PV = constant).
Charles's law: at constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of a gas is directly proportional to its absolute (Kelvin) temperature (V/T = constant). (Equivalently, volume changes by 1/273 of its volume at 0 °C for each 1 °C change.)
(b) When the volume is reduced, the same number of molecules move in a smaller space, so they collide with the walls of the container more frequently. More collisions per unit area per second means a greater pressure (average speed is unchanged because temperature is constant).
(c) Gas volume is directly proportional to temperature only on the absolute scale; Celsius temperatures can be zero or negative, which would give meaningless results (such as zero or negative volume) in the gas equations.
(d) The volume doubles.
questions.explanation: The kinetic theory links pressure to molecular collisions and temperature to average kinetic energy.

questions.text: Which of the following is chiefly responsible for depletion of the ozone layer?
questions.answer: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)
questions.explanation: In the stratosphere, UV light releases chlorine atoms from CFCs, and these destroy ozone molecules in a chain reaction.

questions.text: The protective ozone layer lies in the ____ region of the atmosphere.
questions.answer: stratosphere
questions.explanation: Stratospheric ozone absorbs most of the harmful ultraviolet radiation from the sun.

questions.text: Name two greenhouse gases and state one consequence of global warming.
questions.answer:
Greenhouse gases (any two): carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄), nitrous oxide (N₂O), water vapour, CFCs.
Consequence (any one): melting of glaciers and polar ice causing a rise in sea level and flooding of low-lying areas; changes in rainfall patterns and more extreme weather; effects on crops and loss of habitats.
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases trap infrared radiation emitted by the earth, raising the average temperature.

questions.text: Explain how acid rain is formed, with balanced equations for the formation of one acid from sulphur dioxide and one from nitrogen dioxide. State one harmful effect of acid rain.
questions.answer:
Sulphur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen released by burning fossil fuels and by industries dissolve in rainwater to form acids.
From SO₂: 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃, then SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄ (or SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃).
From NO₂: 4NO₂ + 2H₂O + O₂ → 4HNO₃.
Harmful effect (any one): corrodes buildings and monuments made of marble or limestone (CaCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂); makes soil and lakes acidic, harming plants and aquatic life; damages leaves of trees; corrodes metal structures.
questions.explanation: Normal rain is slightly acidic due to CO₂; acid rain has a pH well below about 5.6 because of these stronger acids.
